claims.text: Introducing a gradient microstructure can overcome the conventional strength-ductility trade-off.
The proposed gradient consists of a nanostructured, high-strength surface layer transitioning into a ductile core.
The initial bulk material has a homogeneous, coarse-grained microstructure.
Surface mechanical attrition treatment or a similar process can produce a gradient nanostructured surface layer.
The processed surface layer gradually transitions into the unmodified coarse-grained interior.
The proposed response applies under ambient-temperature, quasi-static mechanical testing conditions.
The engineered structure contains a thin, nanostructured, high-strength surface layer over a ductile, coarse-grained core.
The grain-size and structural gradient creates a heterostructure that promotes strain partitioning.
The hard nanostructured surface layer enhances strength.
Interaction between the hard surface layer and the ductile core alleviates strain localization.
Alleviating strain localization enhances strain hardening and ductility.
The gradient-structured material will have greater yield strength than the homogeneous material.
The gradient-structured material will have greater overall ductility than the homogeneous material.
A conventional homogeneous microstructure typically gains strength at the expense of ductility.
The beneficial effects depend on gradient-layer thickness and processing intensity.
An excessively thick or mismatched gradient layer may cause interface failure or excessive stress concentrations.
Prior studies in gradient and heterostructured materials support the proposed mechanism.
